claim: Hepatic TAZ protein level is reduced by more than 50% after 24 hours of fasting relative to ad libitum feeding.
source: Hepatic TAZ protein level was reduced by >50% after 24 hr of fasting, relative to ad libitum feeding (Figure 1A and B).
evidence: Supported by immunoblotting data shown in Figure 1A and quantified in Figure 1B.

claim: The phosphorylation of TAZ at serine 89 is commensurate with the reduction in total TAZ protein during fasting.
source: The phosphorylation of TAZ at serine 89, which is mediated by the Hippo pathway core kinase large tumor suppressor kinase (LATS)1/2 (Lei et al., 2008), was commensurate with the reduction in total TAZ protein (Figure 1A and B).
evidence: Supported by immunoblotting data in Figure 1A and B, and cited reference Lei et al., 2008.

claim: Both nuclear and cytoplasmic TAZ proteins are reduced by fasting.
source: Both nuclear and cytoplasmic TAZ proteins shared this regulation (Figure 1C and D).
evidence: Supported by immunoblotting of nuclear and cytoplasmic extracts shown in Figure 1C and quantified in Figure 1D.

claim: TAZ is abundantly expressed in both the nuclear and cytoplasmic compartments of mature hepatocytes.
source: Immunohistochemistry confirmed that TAZ was abundantly expressed in both the nuclear and cytoplasmic compartments of mature hepatocytes and that its expression was reduced by fasting (Figure 1E).
evidence: Supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: TAZ expression is reduced by fasting as confirmed by immunohistochemistry.
source: Immunohistochemistry confirmed that TAZ was abundantly expressed in both the nuclear and cytoplasmic compartments of mature hepatocytes and that its expression was reduced by fasting (Figure 1E).
evidence: Supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: TAZ shows zonal expression with the highest protein levels in pericentral hepatocytes.
source: Interestingly, TAZ showed zonal expression, with the highest protein levels being found in the pericentral (or perivenous) hepatocytes (Figure 1E).
evidence: Supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: TAZ zonal expression negatively correlates with the expression and activity of gluconeogenic genes in the liver lobule.
source: This zonal expression negatively correlated with the expression and activity of gluconeogenic genes in the liver lobule (Jungermann and Thurman, 1992).
evidence: Inference based on observed zonal expression pattern and cited reference Jungermann and Thurman, 1992.

claim: TAZ is primarily expressed in glutamine synthetase (GLUL)-expressing pericentral hepatocytes.
source: Immunoblotting of isolated pericentral and periportal hepatocytes confirmed that TAZ was primarily expressed in glutamine synthetase (GLUL)-expressing pericentral hepatocytes, whereas YAP is primarily expressed in periportal hepatocytes (Figure 1F).
evidence: Supported by immunoblotting data of isolated pericentral and periportal hepatocytes shown in Figure 1F.

claim: YAP is primarily expressed in periportal hepatocytes.
source: Immunoblotting of isolated pericentral and periportal hepatocytes confirmed that TAZ was primarily expressed in glutamine synthetase (GLUL)-expressing pericentral hepatocytes, whereas YAP is primarily expressed in periportal hepatocytes (Figure 1F).
evidence: Supported by immunoblotting data of isolated pericentral and periportal hepatocytes shown in Figure 1F.

claim: TAZ protein is less abundant in hepatocytes isolated from fasting than ad libitum-fed mice.
source: In addition, TAZ protein was less abundant in hepatocytes isolated from fasting than ad libitum-fed mice (Figure 1G), suggesting that fasting reduces TAZ protein in hepatocytes.
evidence: Supported by immunoblotting data shown in Figure 1G.

claim: Taz mRNA is not affected by fasting or feeding.
source: In contrast to TAZ protein levels, Taz mRNA was not affected by fasting or feeding (Figure 1H), indicating that TAZ is post-transcriptionally regulated by physiological fasting and feeding.
evidence: Supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 1H.

claim: TAZ is post-transcriptionally regulated by physiological fasting and feeding.
source: In contrast to TAZ protein levels, Taz mRNA was not affected by fasting or feeding (Figure 1H), indicating that TAZ is post-transcriptionally regulated by physiological fasting and feeding.
evidence: Inference based on the observation that TAZ protein changes but mRNA does not, shown in Figure 1H.

claim: TAZ protein is induced in mouse primary hepatocyte cultures by supplementation of the medium with high glucose concentration and 10% FBS in a time-dependent manner.
source: Consistent with this, TAZ protein, but not its mRNA, was induced in mouse primary hepatocyte cultures by supplementation of the medium with a high glucose concentration (25 mM) and 10% fetal bovine serum (FBS), which mimics the fed condition, in a time-dependent manner (Figure 1—figure supplement 3A and B).
evidence: Supported by immunoblotting and qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3A and B.

claim: TAZ mRNA is not induced in mouse primary hepatocyte cultures by supplementation of the medium with high glucose concentration and 10% FBS.
source: Consistent with this, TAZ protein, but not its mRNA, was induced in mouse primary hepatocyte cultures by supplementation of the medium with a high glucose concentration (25 mM) and 10% fetal bovine serum (FBS), which mimics the fed condition, in a time-dependent manner (Figure 1—figure supplement 3A and B).
evidence: Supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3B.

claim: Fasting increases the hepatic mRNA expression of Pck1 and G6pc.
source: As expected, fasting increased the hepatic mRNA expression of genes encoding the key gluconeogenic enzymes Pck1 and G6pc, but it inconsistently affected the expression of canonical TAZ and YAP target genes involved in cell proliferation (Patel et al., 2017), including connective tissue growth factor (Ctgf) and cysteine-rich angiogenic inducer 61 (Cyr61) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A and B).
evidence: Supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Fasting inconsistently affects the expression of canonical TAZ and YAP target genes Ctgf and Cyr61.
source: As expected, fasting increased the hepatic mRNA expression of genes encoding the key gluconeogenic enzymes Pck1 and G6pc, but it inconsistently affected the expression of canonical TAZ and YAP target genes involved in cell proliferation (Patel et al., 2017), including connective tissue growth factor (Ctgf) and cysteine-rich angiogenic inducer 61 (Cyr61) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A and B).
evidence: Supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Administration of AdshTAZ to C57BL/6J mice reduces hepatic TAZ mRNA and protein levels.
source: Compared with the control virus, administration of AdshTAZ to C57BL/6J mice reduced hepatic TAZ mRNA and protein levels (Figure 2A and B).
evidence: Supported by qRT-PCR and immunoblotting data shown in Figure 2A and B.

claim: TAZ knockdown does not alter mouse body or epididymal white adipose tissue mass.
source: TAZ knockdown did not alter mouse body or epididymal white adipose tissue mass, but it slightly reduced liver mass, without affecting liver histology (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A–D).
evidence: Supported by measurements shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A and B.

claim: TAZ knockdown slightly reduces liver mass without affecting liver histology.
source: TAZ knockdown did not alter mouse body or epididymal white adipose tissue mass, but it slightly reduced liver mass, without affecting liver histology (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A–D).
evidence: Supported by measurements and histology shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C and D.

claim: TAZ knockdown significantly increases the mRNA expression of hepatic Pck1 by sixfold and G6pc by twofold.
source: However, TAZ knockdown significantly increased the mRNA expression of hepatic Pck1 and G6pc by six- and twofold (Figure 2C), respectively, and PCK1 and G6PC protein levels twofold (Figure 2D and E).
evidence: Supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: TAZ knockdown increases PCK1 and G6PC protein levels twofold.
source: However, TAZ knockdown significantly increased the mRNA expression of hepatic Pck1 and G6pc by six- and twofold (Figure 2C), respectively, and PCK1 and G6PC protein levels twofold (Figure 2D and E).
evidence: Supported by immunoblotting data shown in Figure 2D and quantified in Figure 2E.

claim: Knockdown of hepatic TAZ significantly increases ad libitum-fed and fasting blood glucose concentrations.
source: Consistent with this, knockdown of hepatic TAZ significantly increased the ad libitum-fed and fasting blood glucose concentrations (Figure 2F).
evidence: Supported by blood glucose measurements shown in Figure 2F.

claim: Mice with hepatic TAZ knockdown show larger blood glucose excursions than control mice when challenged with pyruvate.
source: Mice with hepatic TAZ knockdown also showed larger blood glucose excursions than control mice when challenged with pyruvate, a gluconeogenic substrate (Figure 2G).
evidence: Supported by pyruvate tolerance test data shown in Figure 2G.

claim: Knockdown of TAZ does not alter the levels of YAP or key gluconeogenic factors (HNF4α, FoxO1, and GR).
source: By contrast, the knockdown of TAZ did not alter the levels of YAP or key gluconeogenic factors (e.g., hepatic nuclear receptor alpha [HNF4α], forkhead box O1 [FoxO1], and GR; Goldstein and Hager, 2015), suggesting that the inhibition of gluconeogenic gene by TAZ is unlikely to occur via regulation of the protein levels of these key transcription factors (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by immunoblotting data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: TAZ knockdown has little effect on the phosphorylation of AKT, FoxO1, and CREB.
source: It also had little effect on the phosphorylation of AKT, FoxO1, and CREB (Figure 2—figure supplement 2), or on the plasma concentrations of insulin or glucagon (Figure 2—figure supplement 3A and B), hormones that regulate gluconeogenic gene expression.
evidence: Supported by immunoblotting data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: TAZ knockdown has little effect on the plasma concentrations of insulin or glucagon.
source: It also had little effect on the phosphorylation of AKT, FoxO1, and CREB (Figure 2—figure supplement 2), or on the plasma concentrations of insulin or glucagon (Figure 2—figure supplement 3A and B), hormones that regulate gluconeogenic gene expression.
evidence: Supported by ELISA measurements shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3A and B.

claim: L-TAZ KO mice are born at Mendelian ratios.
source: L-TAZ KO mice were born at Mendelian ratios and showed little difference in body mass from sex and age-matched littermate floxed controls (Flox) (Figure 2—figure supplement 4A).
evidence: Observation reported in the text.

claim: L-TAZ KO mice show little difference in body mass from sex and age-matched littermate floxed controls.
source: L-TAZ KO mice were born at Mendelian ratios and showed little difference in body mass from sex and age-matched littermate floxed controls (Flox) (Figure 2—figure supplement 4A).
evidence: Supported by body weight measurements shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 4A.

claim: Knockout of TAZ has no overt effects on liver mass or histology.
source: The knockout of TAZ also had no overt effects on liver mass or histology (Figure 2—figure supplement 4B and C).
evidence: Supported by liver weight measurements and histology shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 4B and C.

claim: L-TAZ KO mice do not have differing levels of IRS1 and 2 expression or insulin sensitivity relative to floxed controls.
source: However, L-TAZ KO mice did not have differing levels of IRS1 and 2 expression or insulin sensitivity relative to floxed controls (Figure 2—figure supplement 5A-C).
evidence: Supported by immunoblotting and insulin tolerance test data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 5A-C.

claim: Both male and female L-TAZ KO mice have higher ad libitum-fed and fasting blood glucose concentrations.
source: Nonetheless, similar to the aforementioned AdshTAZ-treated mice, both male and female L-TAZ KO mice had higher ad libitum-fed and fasting blood glucose concentrations (Figure 2J and K).
evidence: Supported by blood glucose measurements shown in Figure 2J and K.

claim: L-TAZ KO mice show a larger increase in blood glucose during pyruvate tolerance testing.
source: These knockout mice also showed a larger increase in blood glucose during pyruvate tolerance testing (PTT) (Figure 2L and M).
evidence: Supported by pyruvate tolerance test data shown in Figure 2L and M.

claim: Deletion of hepatic TAZ produces a fasting-like state in the liver, in which gluconeogenic gene expression and glucose production are induced.
source: Taken together, these data show that deletion of hepatic TAZ produces a fasting-like state in the liver, in which gluconeogenic gene expression and glucose production are induced.
evidence: Inference based on the collective data from TAZ knockdown and knockout experiments.

claim: AdTAZ administration causes relative hypoglycemia during fasting.
source: Compared with the administration of control virus expressing green fluorescent protein (AdGFP), AdTAZ administration caused relative hypoglycemia during fasting (Figure 3C), which was accompanied by lower mRNA expression and protein levels of hepatic PCK1 and G6PC (Figure 3D and E).
evidence: Supported by blood glucose measurements shown in Figure 3C.

claim: AdTAZ administration is accompanied by lower mRNA expression and protein levels of hepatic PCK1 and G6PC.
source: Compared with the administration of control virus expressing green fluorescent protein (AdGFP), AdTAZ administration caused relative hypoglycemia during fasting (Figure 3C), which was accompanied by lower mRNA expression and protein levels of hepatic PCK1 and G6PC (Figure 3D and E).
evidence: Supported by qRT-PCR and immunoblotting data shown in Figure 3D and E.

claim: TAZ overexpression does not affect mouse body or white adipose mass, but modestly increases liver mass without affecting liver histology.
source: TAZ overexpression did not affect mouse body or white adipose mass, but modestly increased liver mass, without affecting liver histology (Figure 3—figure supplement 2A–D).
evidence: Supported by measurements and histology shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2A–D.

claim: TAZ overexpression blunts the rise in blood glucose caused by the injection of glucagon or pyruvate.
source: TAZ overexpression also blunted the rise in blood glucose caused by the injection of glucagon or pyruvate (Figure 3G and H), without affecting the protein levels of key gluconeogenic factors, the phosphorylation of AKT or CREB, or plasma insulin or glucagon concentrations (Figure 3—figure supplement 2E and F).
evidence: Supported by glucagon challenge and pyruvate tolerance test data shown in Figure 3G and H.

claim: TAZ overexpression does not affect the protein levels of key gluconeogenic factors, the phosphorylation of AKT or CREB, or plasma insulin or glucagon concentrations.
source: TAZ overexpression also blunted the rise in blood glucose caused by the injection of glucagon or pyruvate (Figure 3G and H), without affecting the protein levels of key gluconeogenic factors, the phosphorylation of AKT or CREB, or plasma insulin or glucagon concentrations (Figure 3—figure supplement 2E and F).
evidence: Supported by immunoblotting and ELISA data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2E and F.

claim: Overexpression of TAZ in the fasting state mimics the fed state and is sufficient to inhibit hepatic gluconeogenic gene expression and glucose production.
source: Taken together, these data indicate that the overexpression of TAZ in the fasting state mimics the fed state and is sufficient to inhibit hepatic gluconeogenic gene expression and glucose production.
evidence: Inference based on the collective data from TAZ overexpression experiments.

claim: Infection of mouse primary hepatocytes with AdshTAZ reduces both TAZ mRNA expression and protein level.
source: Infection of mouse primary hepatocytes with AdshTAZ reduced both TAZ mRNA expression and protein level (Figure 4A) and markedly increased the glucagon and dexamethasone (Dex)-induced mRNA expression of Pck1 and G6pc (Figure 4B and C).
evidence: Supported by qRT-PCR and immunoblotting data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: TAZ knockdown markedly increases the glucagon and dexamethasone-induced mRNA expression of Pck1 and G6pc in primary hepatocytes.
source: Infection of mouse primary hepatocytes with AdshTAZ reduced both TAZ mRNA expression and protein level (Figure 4A) and markedly increased the glucagon and dexamethasone (Dex)-induced mRNA expression of Pck1 and G6pc (Figure 4B and C).
evidence: Supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 4B and C.

claim: TAZ knockdown increases glucose secretion into the medium by glucagon-stimulated hepatocytes.
source: TAZ knockdown also increased glucose secretion into the medium by glucagon-stimulated hepatocytes (Figure 4D), which demonstrates the functional importance of these changes in gene expression.
evidence: Supported by glucose production assay data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Infection of mouse primary hepatocytes with AdTAZ increases TAZ protein levels threefold compared with infection with control AdGFP.
source: Conversely, the infection of mouse primary hepatocytes with AdTAZ increased TAZ protein levels threefold compared with infection with control AdGFP (Figure 4E) and substantially inhibited the glucagon and Dex-induced mRNA expression of Pck1 and G6pc (Figure 4F and G).
evidence: Supported by immunoblotting data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: AdTAZ infection substantially inhibits the glucagon and Dex-induced mRNA expression of Pck1 and G6pc in primary hepatocytes.
source: Conversely, the infection of mouse primary hepatocytes with AdTAZ increased TAZ protein levels threefold compared with infection with control AdGFP (Figure 4E) and substantially inhibited the glucagon and Dex-induced mRNA expression of Pck1 and G6pc (Figure 4F and G).
evidence: Supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 4F and G.

claim: AdTAZ infection reduces glucose production after glucagon stimulation in primary hepatocytes.
source: Consistent with these data, AdTAZ infection also reduced glucose production after glucagon stimulation (Figure 4H).
evidence: Supported by glucose production assay data shown in Figure 4H.

claim: AdTAZ blunts the effect of Dex on the induction of the mRNA expression of glycogen synthase 2 (Gys2).
source: In addition to gluconeogenic genes, AdTAZ blunted the effect of Dex on the induction of the mRNA expression of glycogen synthase 2 (Gys2), a GR target gene involved in glycogen metabolism (Bose et al., 2016; Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1 and cited reference Bose et al., 2016.

claim: Knockdown or overexpression of TAZ does not alter the protein levels of YAP or gluconeogenic transcription factors in primary hepatocytes.
source: In addition, knockdown or overexpression of TAZ did not alter the protein levels of YAP or gluconeogenic transcription factors (Figure 4—figure supplement 2A and B).
evidence: Supported by immunoblotting data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2A and B.

claim: TAZ has no effects on either the basal or stimulated phosphorylation of CREB or AKT in hepatocytes treated with glucagon or insulin.
source: Given that insulin and glucagon are major regulators of gluconeogenic genes, we determined whether TAZ regulates their action in hepatocytes and found that it had no effects on either the basal or stimulated phosphorylation of CREB or AKT in hepatocytes treated with glucagon or insulin, respectively (Figure 4—figure supplement 3A-D), suggesting that TAZ is unlikely to directly affect gluconeogenic gene expression by altering the cellular sensitivity to these hormones in hepatocytes.
evidence: Supported by immunoblotting data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3A-D.

claim: TAZ is unlikely to directly affect gluconeogenic gene expression by altering the cellular sensitivity to insulin or glucagon in hepatocytes.
source: Given that insulin and glucagon are major regulators of gluconeogenic genes, we determined whether TAZ regulates their action in hepatocytes and found that it had no effects on either the basal or stimulated phosphorylation of CREB or AKT in hepatocytes treated with glucagon or insulin, respectively (Figure 4—figure supplement 3A-D), suggesting that TAZ is unlikely to directly affect gluconeogenic gene expression by altering the cellular sensitivity to these hormones in hepatocytes.
evidence: Inference based on the lack of effect on CREB and AKT phosphorylation shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3A-D.

claim: Overexpression of TAZ in HepG2 cells inhibits the activity of the G6PC and PCK1 promoters by 50%.
source: Overexpression of TAZ in these cells inhibited the activity of the G6PC and PCK1 promoters by 50% (Figure 5A, Figure 5—figure supplement 1A), indicating that TAZ suppresses transcription of these genes.
evidence: Supported by luciferase reporter assay data shown in Figure 5A and Figure 5—figure supplement 1A.

claim: TAZS89A and TAZS51A mutants inhibit G6PC-Luc to a similar extent compared to wild-type TAZ.
source: To determine whether the Hippo pathway and TEADs are required for these effects of TAZ, we utilized TAZS89A (Lei et al., 2008) and TAZS51A (Zhang et al., 2009) mutants, which abolish TAZ phosphorylation by LATS1/2 and cannot interact with TEADs, respectively. Both mutants inhibited G6PC-Luc to a similar extent, compared to wild-type TAZ (Figure 5A), suggesting that the Hippo pathway and TEADs are not required.
evidence: Supported by luciferase reporter assay data shown in Figure 5A and cited references Lei et al., 2008 and Zhang et al., 2009.

claim: The Hippo pathway and TEADs are not required for TAZ inhibition of G6PC promoter activity.
source: To determine whether the Hippo pathway and TEADs are required for these effects of TAZ, we utilized TAZS89A (Lei et al., 2008) and TAZS51A (Zhang et al., 2009) mutants, which abolish TAZ phosphorylation by LATS1/2 and cannot interact with TEADs, respectively. Both mutants inhibited G6PC-Luc to a similar extent, compared to wild-type TAZ (Figure 5A), suggesting that the Hippo pathway and TEADs are not required.
evidence: Inference based on the observation that TAZS89A and TAZS51A mutants inhibit G6PC-Luc similarly to wild-type TAZ, shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Transfection of cells with a vector expressing an shRNA targeting human TAZ increases the activity of G6PC-Luc and PCK1-Luc by more than 40%.
source: Conversely, the transfection of cells with a vector expressing an shRNA targeting human TAZ reduced TAZ expression (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B) and increased the activity of G6PC-Luc and PCK1-Luc by >40% (Figure 5B, Figure 5—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Supported by luciferase reporter assay data shown in Figure 5B and Figure 5—figure supplement 1C.

claim: TAZ suppresses Dex-stimulated GRE-Luc activity by more than 50%.
source: Similar to our findings using G6PC-Luc and PCK1-Luc, TAZ suppressed Dex-stimulated GRE-Luc activity by >50%, whereas knockdown of TAZ increased promoter activity by 40% (Figure 5C and D), suggesting that TAZ inhibits GR transactivation.
evidence: Supported by luciferase reporter assay data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Knockdown of TAZ increases GRE-Luc promoter activity by 40%.
source: Similar to our findings using G6PC-Luc and PCK1-Luc, TAZ suppressed Dex-stimulated GRE-Luc activity by >50%, whereas knockdown of TAZ increased promoter activity by 40% (Figure 5C and D), suggesting that TAZ inhibits GR transactivation.
evidence: Supported by luciferase reporter assay data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: TAZ inhibits GR transactivation.
source: Similar to our findings using G6PC-Luc and PCK1-Luc, TAZ suppressed Dex-stimulated GRE-Luc activity by >50%, whereas knockdown of TAZ increased promoter activity by 40% (Figure 5C and D), suggesting that TAZ inhibits GR transactivation.
evidence: Inference based on the observation that TAZ suppresses GRE-Luc activity, shown in Figure 5C and D.

claim: TAZ, but not YAP, is able to interact with GR.
source: Co-immunoprecipitation (co-IP) assay revealed that TAZ, but not YAP, was able to interact with GR (Figure 5E).
evidence: Supported by co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 5E.

claim: A TAZ mutant protein lacking the WW domain (TAZΔWW) shows much weaker interaction with GR.
source: A TAZ mutant protein lacking the WW domain (TAZΔWW), but not one lacking the coiled-coil (CC) domain (TAZΔCC), showed much weaker interaction with GR (Figure 5F) and was unable to inhibit GRE-Luc (Figure 5G).
evidence: Supported by co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 5F.

claim: TAZΔWW is unable to inhibit GRE-Luc.
source: A TAZ mutant protein lacking the WW domain (TAZΔWW), but not one lacking the coiled-coil (CC) domain (TAZΔCC), showed much weaker interaction with GR (Figure 5F) and was unable to inhibit GRE-Luc (Figure 5G).
evidence: Supported by luciferase reporter assay data shown in Figure 5G.

claim: TAZS89A suppresses glucagon or Dex-induced activation of Pck1 and G6pc gene expression by more than 80% in primary mouse hepatocytes.
source: Consistent with this, compared with the TAZS89A mutant that suppressed glucagon or Dex-induced activation of Pck1 and G6pc gene expression by >80% in primary mouse hepatocytes, TAZΔWW failed to suppress glucagon or Dex-induced Pck1 and G6pc expression (Figure 5H–J).
evidence: Supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 5I and J.

claim: TAZΔWW fails to suppress glucagon or Dex-induced Pck1 and G6pc expression in primary mouse hepatocytes.
source: Consistent with this, compared with the TAZS89A mutant that suppressed glucagon or Dex-induced activation of Pck1 and G6pc gene expression by >80% in primary mouse hepatocytes, TAZΔWW failed to suppress glucagon or Dex-induced Pck1 and G6pc expression (Figure 5H–J).
evidence: Supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 5I and J.

claim: A TAZ mutant consisting of only the WW domain (TAZWW) is sufficient to inhibit G6PC-Luc and GRE-Luc activity.
source: Furthermore, a TAZ mutant consisting of only the WW domain (TAZWW) was sufficient to inhibit G6PC-Luc and GRE-Luc activity (Figure 5K and L), but was unable to activate TEAD, due to the lack of a TEAD-binding domain (Figure 5—figure supplement 2), suggesting that the effects of TAZ on gluconeogenic genes can be separated from its effects on proliferative genes.
evidence: Supported by luciferase reporter assay data shown in Figure 5K and L.

claim: TAZWW is unable to activate TEAD due to the lack of a TEAD-binding domain.
source: Furthermore, a TAZ mutant consisting of only the WW domain (TAZWW) was sufficient to inhibit G6PC-Luc and GRE-Luc activity (Figure 5K and L), but was unable to activate TEAD, due to the lack of a TEAD-binding domain (Figure 5—figure supplement 2), suggesting that the effects of TAZ on gluconeogenic genes can be separated from its effects on proliferative genes.
evidence: Supported by luciferase reporter assay data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: The effects of TAZ on gluconeogenic genes can be separated from its effects on proliferative genes.
source: Furthermore, a TAZ mutant consisting of only the WW domain (TAZWW) was sufficient to inhibit G6PC-Luc and GRE-Luc activity (Figure 5K and L), but was unable to activate TEAD, due to the lack of a TEAD-binding domain (Figure 5—figure supplement 2), suggesting that the effects of TAZ on gluconeogenic genes can be separated from its effects on proliferative genes.
evidence: Inference based on the observation that TAZWW inhibits gluconeogenic gene promoters but cannot activate TEAD, shown in Figure 5K, L, and Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: A GR mutant in which the conserved IPKY motif was mutated to alanines (GR4A mutant) interacts with TAZ much more weakly.
source: Conversely, a GR mutant in which the conserved IPKY motif was mutated to alanines (A) (GR4A mutant) interacted with TAZ much more weakly, despite being expressed at a level similar to that of the wild-type GR (Figure 5M).
evidence: Supported by co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 5M.

claim: The GR4A mutant is not subject to TAZ-mediated inhibition of GRE-Luc and displays a greater ability to induce the activities of the GRE-Luc and G6PC-Luc reporters.
source: In addition, compared with wild-type GR, the GR4A mutant was not subject to TAZ-mediated inhibition of GRE-Luc and displayed a greater ability to induce the activities of the GRE-Luc and G6PC-Luc reporters (Figure 5N and O).
evidence: Supported by luciferase reporter assay data shown in Figure 5N and O.

claim: Overexpression of TAZ has little effect on GR subcellular distribution in either the absence or presence of Dex.
source: Whereas Dex treatment induced the nuclear accumulation of GR, overexpression of TAZ had little effect on its subcellular distribution in either the absence or presence of Dex (Figure 5—figure supplement 3A).
evidence: Supported by fluorescence microscopy data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 3A.

claim: TAZ does not reduce the quantity of dimeric GR in cells.
source: Similarly, TAZ did not reduce the quantity of dimeric GR in cells, as shown by immunoblotting after the treatment of cells with a cross-linker (dithiobis [succinimidyl propionate] [DSP]) (Figure 5—figure supplement 3B).
evidence: Supported by immunoblotting data after DSP cross-linking shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 3B.

claim: The TAZ-GR interaction does not impair GR nuclear localization, ligand activation, or dimerization.
source: In addition, the fact that the GR4A mutant can be activated by Dex (Figure 5N and O) also suggests that the TAZ-GR interaction does not impair GR nuclear localization, ligand activation, or dimerization.
evidence: Inference based on the observation that the GR4A mutant, which does not interact with TAZ, can still be activated by Dex, shown in Figure 5N and O.

claim: Glucagon treatment strongly promotes the binding of GR to the Pck1 and G6pc promoter regions containing GREs.
source: Glucagon treatment strongly promoted the binding of GR to the Pck1 and G6pc promoter regions containing GREs ('Pck1 (GRE)', −376 to −280 and 'G6pc (GRE)', −215 to −111), but not to a distal region of the Pck1 promoter lacking GREs ('Pck1 (Con)', −3678 to −3564).
evidence: Supported by ChIP assay data described in the text.

claim: The glucagon-induced binding of GR to the Pck1 or G6pc promoters is significantly lower in cells overexpressing TAZ.
source: However, the glucagon-induced binding of GR to the Pck1 or G6pc promoters was significantly lower in cells overexpressing TAZ (Figure 5P).
evidence: Supported by ChIP assay data shown in Figure 5P.

claim: The TAZ-GR interaction limits gluconeogenic gene expression by reducing GR binding to GREs.
source: Taken together, these data suggest that the TAZ-GR interaction limits gluconeogenic gene expression by reducing GR binding to GREs.
evidence: Inference based on the collective data showing TAZ reduces GR binding to GREs.

claim: RU486 blocks the interaction of GR with TAZ.
source: Interestingly, we found that RU486 blocked the interaction of GR with TAZ (Figure 5Q), probably due to the change in GR conformation.
evidence: Supported by co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 5Q.

claim: RU486 treatment of hepatocytes reduces glucagon-stimulated Pck1 and G6pc mRNA expression.
source: As expected, RU486 treatment of hepatocytes reduced glucagon-stimulated Pck1 and G6pc mRNA expression (Figure 5R and S), whereas the knockdown of TAZ increased glucagon-stimulated Pck1 and G6pc expression in the absence of RU486.
evidence: Supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 5R and S.

claim: RU486 entirely abolishes the increase in glucagon-stimulated Pck1 and G6pc expression caused by TAZ knockdown.
source: However, this increase was entirely abolished in the presence of RU486 (Figure 5R).
evidence: Supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 5R.

claim: RU486 prevents the inhibitory effects of TAZ overexpression on Pck1 and G6pc expression in hepatocytes.
source: Similarly, RU486 prevented the inhibitory effects of TAZ overexpression on Pck1 and G6pc expression in hepatocytes (Figure 5S).
evidence: Supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 5S.

claim: The TAZ-GR interaction is necessary for the reduction in gluconeogenic gene expression.
source: Thus, not only is the TAZ-GR interaction necessary for the reduction in gluconeogenic gene expression, but it is likely the sole mechanism for such a reduction.
evidence: Inference based on the observation that RU486, which blocks TAZ-GR interaction, abolishes TAZ effects on gluconeogenic gene expression.

claim: The TAZ-GR interaction is likely the sole mechanism for TAZ-mediated reduction in gluconeogenic gene expression.
source: Thus, not only is the TAZ-GR interaction necessary for the reduction in gluconeogenic gene expression, but it is likely the sole mechanism for such a reduction.
evidence: Inference based on the observation that RU486, which blocks TAZ-GR interaction, abolishes TAZ effects on gluconeogenic gene expression.

claim: GR in the nuclear extracts of wild-type mouse liver can be immunoprecipitated using an antibody targeting endogenous TAZ.
source: Consistent with the interaction between GR and TAZ identified in cultured cells, GR in the nuclear extracts of wild-type mouse liver could be immunoprecipitated using an antibody targeting endogenous TAZ (Figure 6A).
evidence: Supported by co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: GR binds to regions of the G6pc and Pck1 promoters containing functional GREs in mouse liver.
source: GR bound to regions of the G6pc and Pck1 promoters containing functional GREs (Figure 6B).
evidence: Supported by ChIP assay data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: The binding of GR to GRE-containing regions of the G6pc and Pck1 promoters is significantly increased by TAZ knockdown in mouse liver.
source: The binding of GR to GRE-containing regions of the G6pc and Pck1 promoters was significantly increased by TAZ knockdown (Figure 6B).
evidence: Supported by ChIP assay data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: The histone acetylation of G6pc and Pck1 promoter regions containing or near to GREs is increased 50–80% by TAZ knockdown in mouse liver.
source: Moreover, the histone acetylation of G6pc and Pck1 promoter regions containing or near to GREs was increased 50–80% by TAZ knockdown (Figure 6C), implying active transcription from the G6pc and Pck1 genes.
evidence: Supported by ChIP assay data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: TAZ overexpression causes a 25–45% reduction in the binding of GR to GREs in mouse liver.
source: Conversely, ChIP assays revealed that TAZ overexpression caused a 25–45% reduction in the binding of GR to GREs, histone acetylation, and the binding of the polymerase II subunit (Pol II) to the promoter regions of G6pc and Pck1 (Figure 6D–F).
evidence: Supported by ChIP assay data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: TAZ overexpression causes a 25–45% reduction in histone acetylation of the promoter regions of G6pc and Pck1 in mouse liver.
source: Conversely, ChIP assays revealed that TAZ overexpression caused a 25–45% reduction in the binding of GR to GREs, histone acetylation, and the binding of the polymerase II subunit (Pol II) to the promoter regions of G6pc and Pck1 (Figure 6D–F).
evidence: Supported by ChIP assay data shown in Figure 6E.

claim: TAZ overexpression causes a 25–45% reduction in the binding of Pol II to the promoter regions of G6pc and Pck1 in mouse liver.
source: Conversely, ChIP assays revealed that TAZ overexpression caused a 25–45% reduction in the binding of GR to GREs, histone acetylation, and the binding of the polymerase II subunit (Pol II) to the promoter regions of G6pc and Pck1 (Figure 6D–F).
evidence: Supported by ChIP assay data shown in Figure 6F.

claim: TAZ binds normally to the promoter of Ctgf but not to the promoters of G6pc or Pck1 in AdTAZ-infected mice.
source: However, TAZ bound normally to the promoter of Ctgf (a well-described TAZ target gene that is not known to be regulated by GR) in AdTAZ-infected mice, but not to the promoters of G6pc or Pck1 (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by ChIP assay data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: TAZ inhibits GR transactivation by interacting with GR and suppressing GR binding to GREs, rather than by binding near or within GREs.
source: These data support a model in which TAZ inhibits GR transactivation by interacting with GR and suppressing GR binding to GREs, rather than a model in which TAZ binding near or within GREs inhibits the binding of GR to gluconeogenic gene promoters.
evidence: Inference based on the observation that TAZ does not bind to G6pc or Pck1 promoters but does bind to Ctgf promoter, shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: RU486 reduces the TAZ-GR interaction in mouse liver nuclear extracts.
source: Because RU486 reduced the TAZ-GR interaction in cultured cells (Figure 5Q) and mouse liver nuclear extracts (Figure 6G), we determined whether RU486 could abrogate the effects of TAZ on glucose homeostasis in mice.
evidence: Supported by co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 6G.

claim: RU486 treatment completely abolishes the increase in blood glucose caused by TAZ knockdown in mice.
source: As expected, TAZ knockdown increased mouse blood glucose concentration prior to RU486 injection. However, this increase was completely abolished by RU486 treatment (Figure 6H).
evidence: Supported by blood glucose measurements shown in Figure 6H.

claim: RU486 treatment abolishes the effects of hepatic TAZ knockout on fasting blood glucose in mice.
source: Similarly, hepatic TAZ knockout increased fasting blood glucose and glucose production after pyruvate administration to mice; and RU486 treatment abolished the effects of TAZ on blood glucose (Figure 6I).
evidence: Supported by blood glucose measurements shown in Figure 6I.

claim: RU486 entirely abolishes the effects of hepatic TAZ knockout on glucose production during pyruvate tolerance testing in mice.
source: RU486 is a GR antagonist, and thus it lowered glucose production in floxed mice during a PTT. Similar to its effect on blood glucose concentration, RU486 entirely abolished the effects of hepatic TAZ knockout on glucose production (Figure 6J).
evidence: Supported by pyruvate tolerance test data shown in Figure 6J.

claim: RU486 entirely abolishes the ability of overexpressed hepatic TAZ to reduce gluconeogenic gene expression, improve pyruvate tolerance, and inhibit gluconeogenic gene expression in mice.
source: Consistent with these loss-of-function studies, RU486 also entirely abolished the ability of overexpressed hepatic TAZ to reduce gluconeogenic gene expression, improve pyruvate tolerance, and inhibit gluconeogenic gene expression (Figure 6K–M).
evidence: Supported by blood glucose, pyruvate tolerance test, and qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 6K–M.

claim: RU486 abolishes the ability of TAZ to reduce GR binding to GREs in the Pck1 or G6pc promoters and the amounts of acetylated histones on these promoters in mouse liver.
source: Moreover, RU486 abolished the ability of TAZ to reduce GR binding to GREs in the Pck1 or G6pc promoters and the amounts of acetylated histones on these promoters (Figure 6N).
evidence: Supported by ChIP assay data shown in Figure 6N.

claim: The interaction between GR and TAZ is required for the inhibitory effects of TAZ on hepatic gluconeogenic gene expression in mice.
source: These data confirm that the interaction between GR and TAZ is required for the inhibitory effects of TAZ on hepatic gluconeogenic gene expression in mice.
evidence: Inference based on the observation that RU486, which blocks TAZ-GR interaction, abolishes TAZ effects on gluconeogenic gene expression in mice.

claim: TAZ overexpression inhibits the Dex-induced increases in blood glucose and gluconeogenic gene expression in mouse liver.
source: TAZ overexpression inhibited the Dex-induced increases in blood glucose and gluconeogenic gene expression, but the effects of TAZ on the inhibition of inflammatory gene expression by Dex, including the expression of the tumor necrosis factor alpha (Tnfα) and interleukin 1 (Il1) genes, were inconsistent (Figure 6—figure supplement 2A and B).
evidence: Supported by blood glucose and qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2A and B.

claim: The effects of TAZ on the inhibition of inflammatory gene expression by Dex are inconsistent.
source: TAZ overexpression inhibited the Dex-induced increases in blood glucose and gluconeogenic gene expression, but the effects of TAZ on the inhibition of inflammatory gene expression by Dex, including the expression of the tumor necrosis factor alpha (Tnfα) and interleukin 1 (Il1) genes, were inconsistent (Figure 6—figure supplement 2A and B).
evidence: Supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2B.

claim: TAZS89A reduces the blood glucose of ad libitum-fed, fasted, or pyruvate-challenged mice.
source: Compared with control AdGFP, TAZS89A reduced the blood glucose of ad libitum-fed, fasted, or pyruvate-challenged mice (Figure 7A and B).
evidence: Supported by blood glucose and pyruvate tolerance test data shown in Figure 7A and B.

claim: TAZΔWW fails to reduce blood glucose and glucose production during PTT in mice.
source: By contrast, TAZΔWW failed to reduce blood glucose and glucose production during PTT (Figure 7A and B), although the TAZΔWW mutant appeared to be more stable in mouse liver (Figure 7—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Supported by blood glucose and pyruvate tolerance test data shown in Figure 7A and B.

claim: The TAZΔWW mutant is more stable in mouse liver than wild-type TAZ.
source: By contrast, TAZΔWW failed to reduce blood glucose and glucose production during PTT (Figure 7A and B), although the TAZΔWW mutant appeared to be more stable in mouse liver (Figure 7—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Supported by immunoblotting data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1C.

claim: The TAZΔWW mutant fails to inhibit Pck1 and G6pc expression in mouse liver.
source: In addition, the TAZΔWW mutant failed to inhibit Pck1 and G6pc expression and the binding of GR to GREs in the Pck1 and G6pc promoters in mouse liver (Figure 7C and D).
evidence: Supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 7C.

claim: The TAZΔWW mutant fails to inhibit the binding of GR to GREs in the Pck1 and G6pc promoters in mouse liver.
source: In addition, the TAZΔWW mutant failed to inhibit Pck1 and G6pc expression and the binding of GR to GREs in the Pck1 and G6pc promoters in mouse liver (Figure 7C and D).
evidence: Supported by ChIP assay data shown in Figure 7D.

claim: The WW domain mediates the inhibition of gluconeogenic gene expression by TAZ in vivo.
source: Taken together, these data suggest that the WW domain mediates the inhibition of gluconeogenic gene expression by TAZ in vivo.
evidence: Inference based on the observation that TAZΔWW fails to inhibit gluconeogenic gene expression in vivo, shown in Figure 7A-D.

claim: The binding of GR to GREs in the G6pc and Pck1 promoters is increased by more than 50% in the livers of mice that were fasted versus those that were fed.
source: Fasting increases GR binding to gluconeogenic gene promoters in mouse liver and feeding reduces this binding (Kalvisa et al., 2018). Consistent with this, we found that the binding of GR to GREs in the G6pc and Pck1 promoters was increased by >50% in the livers of mice that were fasted versus those that were fed (Figure 7E).
evidence: Supported by ChIP assay data shown in Figure 7E and cited reference Kalvisa et al., 2018.

claim: In the fed state, high hepatic TAZ expression inhibits GR transactivation of gluconeogenic genes by interacting with GR and reducing the binding of GR to the promoters of these genes.
source: Collectively, our data suggest a role for hepatic TAZ in glucose homeostasis in normal mouse liver. In the fed state, high hepatic TAZ expression inhibits GR transactivation of gluconeogenic genes by interacting with GR and reducing the binding of GR to the promoters of these genes; whereas in the fasted state, lower TAZ expression enables GR to bind to gluconeogenic genes and activate their transcription, which increases glucose production (Figure 7F).
evidence: Inference based on the collective data presented in the manuscript, summarized in Figure 7F.

claim: In the fasted state, lower TAZ expression enables GR to bind to gluconeogenic genes and activate their transcription, which increases glucose production.
source: Collectively, our data suggest a role for hepatic TAZ in glucose homeostasis in normal mouse liver. In the fed state, high hepatic TAZ expression inhibits GR transactivation of gluconeogenic genes by interacting with GR and reducing the binding of GR to the promoters of these genes; whereas in the fasted state, lower TAZ expression enables GR to bind to gluconeogenic genes and activate their transcription, which increases glucose production (Figure 7F).
evidence: Inference based on the collective data presented in the manuscript, summarized in Figure 7F.

claim: TAZ protein expression is reduced in L-DKO mouse liver.
source: TAZ protein expression was reduced in L-DKO mouse liver (Figure 8—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by immunoblotting data shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1A.

claim: AdTAZS89A reduces blood glucose concentration, glucose production, and gluconeogenic gene expression in both L-DKO and floxed control mice.
source: AdTAZS89A administration affected mouse body and liver mass to a similar extent in both L-DKO and floxed controls (Figure 8—figure supplement 1B and C), and importantly, AdTAZS89A reduced blood glucose concentration, glucose production, and gluconeogenic gene expression in both L-DKO and floxed control mice (Figure 8A–C), suggesting that TAZ overexpression is sufficient to reduce glucose production in these insulin-resistant mice.
evidence: Supported by blood glucose, pyruvate tolerance test, and qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 8A–C.

claim: TAZ overexpression is sufficient to reduce glucose production in insulin-resistant L-DKO mice.
source: AdTAZS89A administration affected mouse body and liver mass to a similar extent in both L-DKO and floxed controls (Figure 8—figure supplement 1B and C), and importantly, AdTAZS89A reduced blood glucose concentration, glucose production, and gluconeogenic gene expression in both L-DKO and floxed control mice (Figure 8A–C), suggesting that TAZ overexpression is sufficient to reduce glucose production in these insulin-resistant mice.
evidence: Inference based on the observation that AdTAZS89A reduces glucose production in L-DKO mice, shown in Figure 8A–C.

claim: High-fat diet increases hepatic TAZ protein level in fasted mice.
source: HFD increased hepatic TAZ protein level in fasted mice, and to a lesser extent in fed mice, and that L-TAZ KO in mice significantly increased glucose production after pyruvate challenge (Figure 8D and E).
evidence: Supported by immunoblotting data shown in Figure 8D.

claim: L-TAZ KO in mice significantly increases glucose production after pyruvate challenge in HFD-fed mice.
source: HFD increased hepatic TAZ protein level in fasted mice, and to a lesser extent in fed mice, and that L-TAZ KO in mice significantly increased glucose production after pyruvate challenge (Figure 8D and E).
evidence: Supported by pyruvate tolerance test data shown in Figure 8E.

claim: L-TAZ KO worsens insulin intolerance in HFD-fed mice.
source: Consistent with this, L-TAZ KO worsened insulin intolerance in these HFD-fed mice (Figure 8F).
evidence: Supported by insulin tolerance test data shown in Figure 8F.

claim: Hepatic TAZ regulates glucose homeostasis in insulin resistance.
source: Taken together, these data suggest that hepatic TAZ regulates glucose homeostasis in insulin resistance.
evidence: Inference based on the collective data from L-DKO and HFD-fed mice experiments.

claim: YAP and TAZ share nearly 50% amino acid sequence similarity.
source: Although YAP and TAZ share nearly 50% amino acid sequence similarity, the two proteins have distinct functions that are exerted via interactions with different transcription factors (Piccolo et al., 2014; Plouffe et al., 2018).
evidence: Established knowledge cited from Piccolo et al., 2014 and Plouffe et al., 2018.

claim: YAP and TAZ have distinct functions that are exerted via interactions with different transcription factors.
source: Although YAP and TAZ share nearly 50% amino acid sequence similarity, the two proteins have distinct functions that are exerted via interactions with different transcription factors (Piccolo et al., 2014; Plouffe et al., 2018).
evidence: Established knowledge cited from Piccolo et al., 2014 and Plouffe et al., 2018.

claim: YAP activates epidermal growth factor receptor 4 (ErbB4) and tumor suppressor p73.
source: For example, YAP activates epidermal growth factor receptor 4 (ErbB4) and tumor suppressor p73 (Komuro et al., 2003; Lapi et al., 2008), whereas TAZ specifically interacts with peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor gamma (PPARγ) and T-box transcription factor (TBX5) (Hong et al., 2005; Murakami et al., 2005).
evidence: Established knowledge cited from Komuro et al., 2003 and Lapi et al., 2008.

claim: TAZ specifically interacts with peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor gamma (PPARγ) and T-box transcription factor (TBX5).
source: For example, YAP activates epidermal growth factor receptor 4 (ErbB4) and tumor suppressor p73 (Komuro et al., 2003; Lapi et al., 2008), whereas TAZ specifically interacts with peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor gamma (PPARγ) and T-box transcription factor (TBX5) (Hong et al., 2005; Murakami et al., 2005).
evidence: Established knowledge cited from Hong et al., 2005 and Murakami et al., 2005.

claim: The binding of TAZ to PPARγ inhibits the PPARγ-induced differentiation of mesenchymal stem cells into adipocytes.
source: In addition, although TAZ co-activates TEADs, it also acts as a repressor: the binding of TAZ to PPARγ inhibits the PPARγ-induced differentiation of mesenchymal stem cells into adipocytes (Hong et al., 2005).
evidence: Established knowledge cited from Hong et al., 2005.

claim: YAP integrates gluconeogenic gene expression and cell proliferation, which contributes to its tumorigenic effects.
source: We previously reported that YAP integrates gluconeogenic gene expression and cell proliferation, which contributes to its tumorigenic effects (Hu et al., 2017).
evidence: Previous findings by the authors cited from Hu et al., 2017.

claim: Hepatocyte-specific deletion of YAP in normal mice has little effect on gluconeogenic gene expression.
source: However, hepatocyte-specific deletion of YAP in normal mice has little effect on gluconeogenic gene expression (Hu et al., 2017).
evidence: Previous findings by the authors cited from Hu et al., 2017.

claim: YAP is primarily expressed in cholangiocytes in normal mouse liver.
source: Whereas YAP is primarily expressed in cholangiocytes in normal mouse liver (Yimlamai et al., 2014), we show here that TAZ is abundantly expressed in pericentral hepatocytes and that its expression is markedly reduced by fasting.
evidence: Established knowledge cited from Yimlamai et al., 2014.

claim: The liver plays a critical role in organismal energy homeostasis by regulating diverse biological processes in response to nutrient availability.
source: The liver plays a critical role in organismal energy homeostasis by regulating diverse biological processes in response to nutrient availability (Rui, 2014).
evidence: Established knowledge cited from Rui, 2014.

claim: During fasting, the activation of hepatic gluconeogenesis is required for the supply of glucose to tissues with a high glucose demand and for the maintenance of glucose homeostasis.
source: During fasting, the activation of hepatic gluconeogenesis is required for the supply of glucose to tissues with a high glucose demand, such as the brain, and for the maintenance of glucose homeostasis, whereas in the fed state gluconeogenesis is suppressed (McGarry et al., 1973; Landau et al., 1996).
evidence: Established knowledge cited from McGarry et al., 1973 and Landau et al., 1996.

claim: In the fed state, gluconeogenesis is suppressed.
source: During fasting, the activation of hepatic gluconeogenesis is required for the supply of glucose to tissues with a high glucose demand, such as the brain, and for the maintenance of glucose homeostasis, whereas in the fed state gluconeogenesis is suppressed (McGarry et al., 1973; Landau et al., 1996).
evidence: Established knowledge cited from McGarry et al., 1973 and Landau et al., 1996.

claim: A failure to suppress hepatic gluconeogenesis postprandially contributes to hyperglycemia in insulin resistance and diabetes.
source: Precise control of hepatic gluconeogenesis is crucial for normal physiology, and a failure to suppress hepatic gluconeogenesis postprandially contributes to hyperglycemia in insulin resistance and diabetes (Magnusson et al., 1992).
evidence: Established knowledge cited from Magnusson et al., 1992.

claim: Glucagon and glucocorticoids are hormones that are secreted during fasting and promote hepatic gluconeogenesis at multiple levels, including via gene transcription.
source: Glucagon and glucocorticoids (GCs; in humans, cortisol; in mice, corticosterone; synthesized in the adrenal cortex) are hormones that are secreted during fasting and promote hepatic gluconeogenesis at multiple levels, including via gene transcription.
evidence: Established knowledge in the field.

claim: Glucocorticoid receptor (GR) is a member of the nuclear receptor super-family.
source: Glucocorticoid receptor (GR, encoded by the NR3C1 gene) is a member of the nuclear receptor super-family (Hollenberg et al., 1985) that is a key transcriptional regulator of gluconeogenic gene expression in the fasting state (Heitzer et al., 2007).
evidence: Established knowledge cited from Hollenberg et al., 1985.

claim: GR is a key transcriptional regulator of gluconeogenic gene expression in the fasting state.
source: Glucocorticoid receptor (GR, encoded by the NR3C1 gene) is a member of the nuclear receptor super-family (Hollenberg et al., 1985) that is a key transcriptional regulator of gluconeogenic gene expression in the fasting state (Heitzer et al., 2007).
evidence: Established knowledge cited from Heitzer et al., 2007.

claim: GR not only directly responds to increases in GC concentration by activating gluconeogenic gene transcription, but also plays a permissive role in the glucagon-mediated transcriptional control of these genes.
source: GR not only directly responds to increases in GC concentration by activating gluconeogenic gene transcription, but also plays a permissive role in the glucagon-mediated transcriptional control of these genes.
evidence: Established knowledge in the field.

claim: The deletion of hepatic GR leads to fasting hypoglycemia.
source: Therefore, the deletion of hepatic GR leads to fasting hypoglycemia (Opherk et al., 2004), while adrenalectomy abrogates the induction of gluconeogenesis by fasting, glucagon, cAMP, or epinephrine in rodents (Exton et al., 1972; Winternitz et al., 1957).
evidence: Established knowledge cited from Opherk et al., 2004.

claim: Adrenalectomy abrogates the induction of gluconeogenesis by fasting, glucagon, cAMP, or epinephrine in rodents.
source: Therefore, the deletion of hepatic GR leads to fasting hypoglycemia (Opherk et al., 2004), while adrenalectomy abrogates the induction of gluconeogenesis by fasting, glucagon, cAMP, or epinephrine in rodents (Exton et al., 1972; Winternitz et al., 1957).
evidence: Established knowledge cited from Exton et al., 1972 and Winternitz et al., 1957.

claim: A single dose of a GR antagonist is sufficient to reduce hepatic glucose output in healthy humans.
source: Similarly, a single dose of a GR antagonist is sufficient to reduce hepatic glucose output in healthy humans (Garrel et al., 1995).
evidence: Established knowledge cited from Garrel et al., 1995.

claim: Upon the binding of a ligand, GR undergoes conformational changes, translocates to the nucleus, dimerizes, and binds to glucocorticoid response elements (GREs) in the promoters of key gluconeogenic genes.
source: Upon the binding of a ligand (a synthetic agonist or an endogenous GC) (Kuo et al., 2015), GR undergoes conformational changes, translocates to the nucleus, dimerizes, and binds to glucocorticoid response elements (GREs) in the promoters of key gluconeogenic genes, such as phosphoenolpyruvate carboxykinase 1 (PCK1) and glucose-6-phosphatase catalytic subunit (G6PC) (Kuo et al., 2015; Vander Kooi et al., 2005), which encode the rate-limiting and final enzymes of gluconeogenesis, respectively (Mutel et al., 2011; She et al., 2000).
evidence: Established knowledge cited from Kuo et al., 2015 and Vander Kooi et al., 2005.

claim: PCK1 and G6PC encode the rate-limiting and final enzymes of gluconeogenesis, respectively.
source: Upon the binding of a ligand (a synthetic agonist or an endogenous GC) (Kuo et al., 2015), GR undergoes conformational changes, translocates to the nucleus, dimerizes, and binds to glucocorticoid response elements (GREs) in the promoters of key gluconeogenic genes, such as phosphoenolpyruvate carboxykinase 1 (PCK1) and glucose-6-phosphatase catalytic subunit (G6PC) (Kuo et al., 2015; Vander Kooi et al., 2005), which encode the rate-limiting and final enzymes of gluconeogenesis, respectively (Mutel et al., 2011; She et al., 2000).
evidence: Established knowledge cited from Mutel et al., 2011 and She et al., 2000.

claim: The transrepression of inflammatory genes by GR involves the tethering of monomeric GR to DNA-bound proinflammatory transcription factors.
source: This activation mechanism differs from that of the transrepression of inflammatory genes by GR, which involves the tethering of monomeric GR to DNA-bound proinflammatory transcription factors (Reichardt et al., 2001).
evidence: Established knowledge cited from Reichardt et al., 2001.
